questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Walk carefully on the wet floor ________ you should slip.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) lest
Why: "Lest" means "for fear that" or "in case"; it is followed by "should" + verb.
Why not the others: (A) means "if not" and reverses the sense. (C) is about time. (D) shows contrast.
Key point: Lest is followed by "should", never by "not".

questions.sub_topic: Antonym pairs: optimist, abundant, victory, ascend
questions.question:
Select the correct pairs of antonyms:
A. optimist — pessimist
B. abundant — plentiful
C. victory — defeat
D. ascend — descend
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: B) A, C and D only
C) B, C and D only
D) A, B, C and D
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A, C and D only
Why: An optimist expects good and a pessimist bad; victory and defeat, and ascend (go up) and descend (go down) are opposites.
Why not the others: Pair B is a pair of synonyms — abundant means plentiful. Options (A), (C) and (D) include pair B.
Key point: Test each pair on its own.

questions.question:
Match the nouns in List-I with the verbs in List-II that they usually go with:

List-I
(A) ____ a crime
(B) ____ a speech
(C) ____ a visit
(D) ____ a promise

List-II
(I) commit
(II) deliver
(III) pay
(IV) keep
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why: Commit a crime (I), deliver a speech (II), pay a visit (III), keep a promise (IV) are fixed collocations.
Why not the others: (B) gives "deliver a crime"; (C) gives "pay a speech"; (D) gives "keep a visit" and "pay a promise".
Key point: Collocations are learnt as pairs.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correctly spelt word to fill in the blank:
The dancers moved to the ________ of the drums.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) rhythm
Why: The correct spelling is r-h-y-t-h-m.
Why not the others: (A) misses the first "h". (C) adds an "e". (D) misses the second "h".
Key point: Rhythm has no vowel except "y" and two Hs.

questions.question:
Select the words that describe "a person who is unable to pay his or her debts":
A. insolvent
B. solvent
C. bankrupt
D. lavish
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, B and C only
C) A, C and D only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A and C only
Why: "Insolvent" and "bankrupt" both describe a person who cannot pay debts.
Why not the others: B (solvent) means able to pay debts — the opposite. D (lavish) means spending a great deal. Options (A), (B) and (C) include one of them.
Key point: The prefix "in-" turns solvent into its opposite.

questions.question:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in capitals:
The villagers were HOSPITABLE to the tired travellers and offered them food and shelter.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Welcoming
Why: Hospitable means friendly and generous to guests; welcoming has the same sense.
Why not the others: (B) is the opposite. (C) does not fit "offered them food and shelter". (D) confuses "hospitable" with "hospital".
Key point: The sentence (food and shelter) confirms the meaning.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to complete the sentence that begins: "The doctor advised him"
A. and to drink plenty of water
B. to rest for a week
C. after the operation
D. to avoid heavy lifting
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) B, D, C, A
Why: "The doctor advised him to rest for a week (B), to avoid heavy lifting (D) after the operation (C), and to drink plenty of water (A)." The final item of a list takes "and".
Why not the others: (A) puts "after the operation" between the first two instructions and leaves the list broken. (B) begins with a time phrase and puts "and" second. (D) begins the list with "and".
Key point: In a list, "and" comes before the last item.

questions.sub_topic: Idioms: storm in a teacup, see eye to eye, eleventh hour, apple of one's eye
questions.question:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) A storm in a teacup
(B) To see eye to eye
(C) At the eleventh hour
(D) The apple of one's eye

List-II
(I) A lot of anger or worry about something unimportant
(II) To agree fully
(III) At the last possible moment
(IV) A person who is loved very much
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why: A storm in a teacup — fuss over a small matter (I); see eye to eye — agree (II); at the eleventh hour — at the last moment (III); the apple of one's eye — someone dearly loved (IV).
Why not the others: (B) swaps the first two; (C) swaps the middle two; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: Learn idioms as whole units of meaning.

questions.question:
Match the words in List-I with their definitions in List-II:

List-I
(A) Amateur
(B) Octogenarian
(C) Polyglot
(D) Plagiarism

List-II
(I) A person who speaks several languages
(II) Copying another person's work and passing it off as one's own
(III) A person who does something for pleasure, not for pay
(IV) A person between eighty and eighty-nine years old
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Amateur — one who does something for pleasure (III); octogenarian — someone in his or her eighties (IV); polyglot — speaker of many languages (I); plagiarism — passing off another's work as one's own (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps amateur and octogenarian; (B) swaps octogenarian and polyglot; (C) swaps the last two.
Key point: "Octo-" means eight; "poly-" means many.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
On his ________ salary, he could barely pay the rent and feed his family.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) meagre
Why: "Meagre" means very small in amount, which fits a salary that barely paid the rent.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) all suggest a large amount, which contradicts "barely".
Key point: "Barely" signals a small amount.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Teaching very young children requires a great deal of ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) patience
Why: After "a great deal of", an uncountable noun is needed: patience, the ability to wait calmly.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) are the adjective and the noun meaning people in hospital. (D) is an adverb.
Key point: Patience (quality) and patients (people) sound alike.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The new rules are ________ only to students who joined after 2025.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) applicable
Why: After "are", an adjective is needed; "applicable to" means relevant to or valid for.
Why not the others: (A) is a verb. (B) is a noun. (D) is an adverb.
Key point: "Be applicable to" someone or something.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
We congratulated her ________ winning the state chess championship.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) on
Why: The verb "congratulate" takes "on": congratulate someone on something.
Why not the others: (B) is common in speech but not standard with "congratulate". (C) and (D) are wrong.
Key point: Congratulate on; thank for.

questions.question:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in capitals:
His FLIMSY excuse for missing the test did not convince the teacher.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Convincing
Why: A flimsy excuse is weak and hard to believe; a convincing one is strong and believable.
Why not the others: (A) is a synonym. (B) and (D) are unrelated in meaning.
Key point: Flimsy can describe things (cloth) or arguments (excuses).

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
You may borrow my notes ________ you return them by Friday.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) as long as
Why: "As long as" means "on the condition that".
Why not the others: (A) shows contrast. (B) shows purpose. (D) must be followed by a noun, not a clause.
Key point: As long as = provided that.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. to sell their vegetables
B. Every Sunday, farmers from nearby villages
C. at the weekly market
D. travel to the town
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) B, D, A, C
Why: The opener with the subject (B) is followed by the verb (D), the purpose (A) and where they sell (C).
Why not the others: (A) puts the purpose before the verb. (C) starts with a lower-case part. (D) puts "at the weekly market" before the verb, so the farmers seem to travel from the market.
Key point: Subject, verb, then purpose and place.

questions.sub_topic: Figures: paradox, pun, transferred epithet, metonymy
questions.question:
Match the figures of speech in List-I with the examples in List-II:

List-I
(A) Paradox
(B) Pun
(C) Transferred epithet
(D) Metonymy

List-II
(I) He spent a sleepless night before the results.
(II) The pen is mightier than the sword.
(III) The more you learn, the more you realise how little you know.
(IV) A bicycle cannot stand on its own because it is two-tyred.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Learning more and knowing less seems self-contradictory but is true — paradox (III); "two-tyred" plays on "too tired" — pun (IV); it is the person, not the night, who is sleepless — transferred epithet (I); "pen" and "sword" stand for writing and war — metonymy (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps paradox and pun; (C) swaps the last two; (D) swaps pun and transferred epithet.
Key point: In a transferred epithet, the adjective belongs to someone other than the noun it describes.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
My grandfather is very fond ________ old Hindi songs.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) of
Why: The fixed expression is "fond of".
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) do not follow "fond".
Key point: Fond of, proud of, afraid of.

questions.sub_topic: The boy whose bicycle was stolen
questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. whose bicycle was stolen
B. went to the police station
C. The boy
D. to file a complaint
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) C, A, B, D
Why: "The boy (C) whose bicycle was stolen (A) went to the police station (B) to file a complaint (D)." The "whose" clause must follow "The boy".
Why not the others: (B) and (D) place the "whose" clause after the police station, as if the station's bicycle was stolen. (C) begins with a lower-case part.
Key point: A relative clause sits right after the noun it describes.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
All ________ must wear their identity cards inside the factory.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) personnel
Why: "Personnel" means the people employed in an organisation.
Why not the others: (B) "Personal" means private or belonging to one person. (C) is an adverb. (D) means a person's character.
Key point: Personnel (double n) are staff; personal (one n) is private.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank:
We ________ milk, so I went to the shop before breakfast.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) had run out of
Why: "Run out of" means to use up a supply completely.
Why not the others: (B) means to meet by chance or to hit. (C) means to knock down with a vehicle. (D) means to chase.
Key point: You run out of milk; you run into a friend.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph:
A. If both Houses pass it, the bill is sent to the President.
B. In India, a new law begins as a bill introduced in Parliament.
C. Once the President gives assent, the bill becomes an Act.
D. It is debated and voted upon in both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) B, D, A, C
Why: B introduces the bill; D says "It is debated ... in both" Houses; A follows ("If both Houses pass it"); C ends with the President's assent.
Why not the others: (A) sends the bill to the President before it is debated. (C) begins with "It". (D) gives the President's assent before the bill is sent to him.
Key point: Pronouns ("It") and conditions ("If both Houses pass it") link the steps.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The judge dismissed the case, calling it a ________ complaint that wasted the court's time.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) frivolous
Why: "Frivolous" means not serious or not important, which fits a complaint that wasted the court's time.
Why not the others: (A) means passionate. (B) means needing hard work. (D) means serious, the opposite.
Key point: The result ("wasted the court's time") points to the word.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. when the lights went out
B. the play
C. Hardly had
D. begun
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) C, B, D, A
Why: "Hardly had (C) the play (B) begun (D) when the lights went out (A)." "Hardly had" is followed by the subject and the past participle, then "when".
Why not the others: (A) puts "when" before the subject. (B) starts with a lower-case part. (C) puts the participle before the subject.
Key point: Hardly had + subject + past participle + when.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank:
While cleaning the cupboard, I ________ an old letter from my grandfather.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) came across
Why: "Come across" means to find or meet by chance.
Why not the others: (A) means to happen. (B) means to regain consciousness or to visit. (C) means to become detached or to succeed.
Key point: Come across = find by chance.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
I am not sure ________ the shop will be open on Sunday.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) whether
Why: "Whether" introduces a choice between possibilities, here open or not open.
Why not the others: (A) "Weather" means the state of the atmosphere. (B) is a male sheep. (D) is an old word meaning "to where".
Key point: Whether = if; weather = rain and sun.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in indirect speech:
She said, "I have finished my homework."
options: A) She said that she had finished her homework.
B) She said that she has finished my homework.
C) She said that I had finished her homework.
D) She said that she finished her homework yesterday.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) She said that she had finished her homework.
Why: With a past reporting verb, the present perfect "have finished" becomes the past perfect "had finished", and "I/my" become "she/her".
Why not the others: (B) keeps "has" and "my". (C) changes the wrong pronoun. (D) changes the tense wrongly and adds a time that was not there.
Key point: Present perfect → past perfect in reported speech.

questions.question: Choose the one word for: "A person who walks in his or her sleep"
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Somnambulist
Why: A somnambulist (Latin "somnus", sleep + "ambulare", to walk) walks while asleep.
Why not the others: (A) cannot sleep. (C) walks, but when awake. (D) puts others into a trance.
Key point: "Ambul-" means walk, as in ambulance (once a walking hospital).

questions.question: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to OPAQUE:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Transparent
Why: Opaque means not letting light through; transparent means letting light through so that one can see clearly.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) are close in meaning to opaque (murky water and impervious walls block light). (D) describes shine, not the passage of light.
Key point: Glass is transparent; wood is opaque.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.sub_topic: Correct sentences: each, scissors, mathematics, look forward to
questions.question:
Which of the following sentences are grammatically correct?
A. Each student must bring his or her own lunch.
B. The scissors is on the table.
C. Mathematics is my favourite subject.
D. I look forward to meet you soon.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, B and C only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A and C only
Why: In A, "each" is singular, so "his or her" is correct. In C, "mathematics" is the name of a subject and takes a singular verb.
Why not the others: B should be "are" ("scissors" is plural). D should be "to meeting" ("to" in "look forward to" is a preposition). Options (A), (B) and (C) include B or D.
Key point: Look forward to + -ing.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to DILIGENT:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Hardworking
Why: Diligent means showing care and steady effort in one's work.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) are good qualities but different ones. (B) is close to the opposite.
Key point: A diligent student does the homework every day.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correctly used word to fill in the blank:
A tall tree in the field was struck by ________ during the storm.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) lightning
Why: "Lightning" (no "e") is the flash of electricity in a storm.
Why not the others: (A) "Lightening" means making lighter. (B) means artificial light or a lighting system. (C) is a verb.
Key point: Thunder and lightning; lightening a load.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in the passive voice:
You must complete the form before the deadline.
options: A) The form must completed by you before the deadline.
B) The form must have completed you before the deadline.
C) The form must be completed by you before the deadline.
D) The form must being completed by you before the deadline.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The form must be completed by you before the deadline.
Why: With a modal verb, the passive is "modal + be + past participle": must be completed.
Why not the others: (A) drops "be". (B) is meaningless. (D) uses "being", which cannot follow "must".
Key point: Can/must/should + be + past participle.

questions.question:
Match the phrasal verbs in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) Bring up
(B) Bring about
(C) Bring out
(D) Bring down

List-II
(I) Cause to happen
(II) Publish or launch
(III) Reduce
(IV) Raise a child, or mention a topic
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
Why: Bring up a child or a topic (IV); bring about change — cause it (I); bring out a new book — publish it (II); bring down prices — reduce them (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps bring up and bring about; (B) swaps bring about and bring out; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: The particle changes the meaning of "bring".

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to SAGACIOUS:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Wise
Why: Sagacious means having good judgement and deep understanding; wise has the same meaning.
Why not the others: (A) is unrelated. (B) means holy and is not the same as wise. (C) is the opposite.
Key point: A sage is a wise person; sagacious comes from the same idea.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

In the dry lands of Gujarat and Rajasthan, rain falls for only a few weeks each year, and for the rest of the year the rivers shrink and the wells run low. For centuries, people here solved the problem in a remarkable way: they built stepwells, known as vav in Gujarati and baori in Rajasthan.

A stepwell is a deep well that people could reach by walking down flights of steps. Instead of lowering a bucket on a rope, villagers went down to the water, however far it had fallen. In the rainy season the well filled almost to the top; in the dry months the water level dropped, and people simply went further down. Because the water lay deep underground, it stayed cool, and the shaded galleries around it became places to rest, meet and celebrate festivals.

Many stepwells were also works of art. The Rani ki Vav at Patan in Gujarat, built in the eleventh century in memory of a king, descends through seven levels and is decorated with hundreds of carved figures of gods, goddesses and dancers. For centuries it lay buried under silt left by floods, until archaeologists cleared it in the twentieth century. In 2014 it was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it now appears on the hundred-rupee note. At Abhaneri in Rajasthan, the Chand Baori has thousands of narrow steps arranged in neat zigzags down thirteen levels.

When piped water and hand pumps arrived, many stepwells fell into neglect and became dumps for rubbish. Today, as cities face water shortages, engineers and citizens are restoring some of them, discovering that these ancient structures were not only beautiful but also a sensible way of saving rain.

Question: According to the passage, where is the Rani ki Vav?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) At Patan in Gujarat
Why: The passage says, "The Rani ki Vav at Patan in Gujarat, built in the eleventh century in memory of a king ..."
Why not the others: (A) is the site of the Chand Baori. (B) and (D) are not mentioned.
Key point: Two examples are given; match each name to its place.

questions.sub_topic: Why steps instead of a bucket
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

In the dry lands of Gujarat and Rajasthan, rain falls for only a few weeks each year, and for the rest of the year the rivers shrink and the wells run low. For centuries, people here solved the problem in a remarkable way: they built stepwells, known as vav in Gujarati and baori in Rajasthan.

In the rainy season the well filled almost to the top; in the dry months the water level dropped, and people simply went further down. Because the water lay deep underground, it stayed cool, and the shaded galleries around it became places to rest, meet and celebrate festivals.

Many stepwells were also works of art. For centuries it lay buried under silt left by floods, until archaeologists cleared it in the twentieth century. In 2014 it was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it now appears on the hundred-rupee note. At Abhaneri in Rajasthan, the Chand Baori has thousands of narrow steps arranged in neat zigzags down thirteen levels.

Today, as cities face water shortages, engineers and citizens are restoring some of them, discovering that these ancient structures were not only beautiful but also a sensible way of saving rain.

Question: Why were the wells built with steps leading down to the water?
options: A) People could reach the water however low it fell
B) Buckets and ropes were too costly for the villagers
C) The steps kept animals away from the drinking water
D) The kings wished to show off their wealth with steps
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) People could reach the water however low it fell
Why: "Villagers went down to the water, however far it had fallen ... in the dry months the water level dropped, and people simply went further down."
Why not the others: (B) and (C) are not stated. (D) Some stepwells were works of art, but that was not why steps were used.
Key point: Look for the problem the design solved.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

For centuries it lay buried under silt left by floods, until archaeologists cleared it in the twentieth century. Today, as cities face water shortages, engineers and citizens are restoring some of them, discovering that these ancient structures were not only beautiful but also a sensible way of saving rain.

Question: "Many stepwells fell into neglect." This means that they:
options: A) Collapsed during floods and earthquakes
B) Were deliberately destroyed by the government
C) Were rebuilt with modern pipes and pumps
D) Were no longer looked after or used properly
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Were no longer looked after or used properly
Why: To fall into neglect is to stop being cared for. The next words, "became dumps for rubbish", confirm it.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are not stated. (C) Pipes replaced the stepwells; the stepwells were not rebuilt with them.
Key point: The words after a phrase often explain it.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

In the rainy season the well filled almost to the top; in the dry months the water level dropped, and people simply went further down. Because the water lay deep underground, it stayed cool, and the shaded galleries around it became places to rest, meet and celebrate festivals.

Many stepwells were also works of art. The Rani ki Vav at Patan in Gujarat, built in the eleventh century in memory of a king, descends through seven levels and is decorated with hundreds of carved figures of gods, goddesses and dancers. For centuries it lay buried under silt left by floods, until archaeologists cleared it in the twentieth century. In 2014 it was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it now appears on the hundred-rupee note. At Abhaneri in Rajasthan, the Chand Baori has thousands of narrow steps arranged in neat zigzags down thirteen levels.

When piped water and hand pumps arrived, many stepwells fell into neglect and became dumps for rubbish. Today, as cities face water shortages, engineers and citizens are restoring some of them, discovering that these ancient structures were not only beautiful but also a sensible way of saving rain.

Question: Which one of these statements does the passage NOT make?
options: A) The Rani ki Vav appears on the hundred-rupee note
B) The Chand Baori was built in memory of a queen
C) The water in stepwells stayed cool
D) Some stepwells are being restored today
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The Chand Baori was built in memory of a queen
Why: The passage says the Rani ki Vav was built "in memory of a king". Nothing is said about why the Chand Baori was built.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are all stated.
Key point: An option may mix a real name with a detail from somewhere else.

questions.sub_topic: What the writer concludes about stepwells
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

In the dry lands of Gujarat and Rajasthan, rain falls for only a few weeks each year, and for the rest of the year the rivers shrink and the wells run low. For centuries, people here solved the problem in a remarkable way: they built stepwells, known as vav in Gujarati and baori in Rajasthan.

A stepwell is a deep well that people could reach by walking down flights of steps. Instead of lowering a bucket on a rope, villagers went down to the water, however far it had fallen. In the rainy season the well filled almost to the top; in the dry months the water level dropped, and people simply went further down. Because the water lay deep underground, it stayed cool, and the shaded galleries around it became places to rest, meet and celebrate festivals.

Many stepwells were also works of art. The Rani ki Vav at Patan in Gujarat, built in the eleventh century in memory of a king, descends through seven levels and is decorated with hundreds of carved figures of gods, goddesses and dancers. For centuries it lay buried under silt left by floods, until archaeologists cleared it in the twentieth century. In 2014 it was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it now appears on the hundred-rupee note. At Abhaneri in Rajasthan, the Chand Baori has thousands of narrow steps arranged in neat zigzags down thirteen levels.

When piped water and hand pumps arrived, many stepwells fell into neglect and became dumps for rubbish. Today, as cities face water shortages, engineers and citizens are restoring some of them, discovering that these ancient structures were not only beautiful but also a sensible way of saving rain.

Question: What does the writer conclude about stepwells in the last paragraph?
options: A) They should be replaced by modern pipes everywhere
B) They are useful today only as tourist attractions
C) They were both beautiful and a sensible way of saving rain
D) They were less useful than hand pumps had been
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) They were both beautiful and a sensible way of saving rain
Why: The passage ends by saying people are "discovering that these ancient structures were not only beautiful but also a sensible way of saving rain".
Why not the others: (A) and (D) reverse the writer's view. (B) Restoration is linked to water shortages, not tourism.
Key point: Conclusions are often stated in the final sentence.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Nani had made besan laddoos every Diwali for fifty years, and every Diwali somebody asked her for the recipe. "There is no recipe," she always said, and laughed.

This year Ishaan, who was sixteen and believed in measurements, decided to write one down. He followed her into the kitchen with a notebook and a pen.

"How much gram flour, Nani?"

She tipped some into the heavy pan without looking. "This much."

"How much is 'this much'?"

"Enough for the family."

Ishaan sighed and weighed what was left in the packet, then did a quick subtraction. "And the ghee?"

"Until the flour stops being thirsty," said Nani, pouring it in a thin golden stream.

She roasted the flour on a low flame, stirring slowly, while Ishaan stood ready with his pen. Five minutes passed, then ten, then fifteen. "When is it done?"

"When the whole house knows," she said.

He was about to protest when the smell reached him: warm, nutty and sweet, like every Diwali he could remember. From the next room his little sister shouted, "Nani is making laddoos!"

Nani smiled at him. "There," she said. "Now it is done."

That night Ishaan copied his notes neatly. He had grams and minutes and temperatures. But at the bottom of the page, in brackets, he added a line no cookbook would have printed: "Roast until the house knows."

Question: What did Nani always say when somebody asked her for the recipe?
options: C) "Ask Ishaan to write it down."
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) "There is no recipe."
Why: The passage says: "'There is no recipe,' she always said, and laughed."
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are never said.
Key point: Quote-based detail questions need the exact words.

Question: "Until the flour stops being thirsty," says Nani about the ghee. She means:
options: A) The flour must be soaked in water first
B) Ghee should be added until the flour has absorbed enough
C) The flour is too dry and should be thrown away
D) Ishaan should bring her a glass of water
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ghee should be added until the flour has absorbed enough
Why: Dry flour soaks up ghee; once it has absorbed enough, it is no longer "thirsty". Nani measures by what she sees, not by weight.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) take the phrase literally or misread it.
Key point: Figurative phrases are explained by the action around them.

Question: What contrast does the story draw between Ishaan and Nani?
options: A) He trusts exact measures; she cooks by experience
B) He is a good cook; she has forgotten how to cook
C) He dislikes laddoos; she makes them only for him
D) He is patient; she is in a hurry to finish
questions.explanation:

Why: Ishaan "believed in measurements" and weighs the packet, while Nani pours "without looking" and judges by smell.

Question: "When the whole house knows," says Nani, when Ishaan asks when the flour is done. What does she mean?

C) When fifteen minutes have passed on the clock

questions.explanation:

Why: Soon afterwards "the smell reached him", and his sister in the next room shouted that Nani was making laddoos. The smell tells the whole house.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are not suggested. (C) Time passes, but Nani does not use the clock.
Key point: The story itself answers what a riddle-like line means.

questions.sub_topic: Figure in stars burn like lanterns
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Night in the Desert

When the last camel bell has faded
and the dunes have given back the heat,
the sky comes down so close above us
it almost touches the sand at our feet.

No city glare, no lamp, no window —
only the dark, so deep and wide
that every star burns like a lantern
somebody forgot to hide.

The Milky Way, a road of silver,
runs from one horizon to the other;
my grandfather points out the Seven Sages,
just as he learnt them from his mother.

A shooting star slides down the darkness,
quick as a match struck and gone;
I make a wish, and keep it secret,
the way that wishes must be done.

And lying there on the cooling sand,
so small beneath that endless sky,
I feel, somehow, not less but larger,
as if the stars were watching, and so was I.

Question: "Every star burns like a lantern / somebody forgot to hide." The figure of speech used here is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Simile
Why: The stars are compared to lanterns using "like" — a simile.
Why not the others: (B) A metaphor does not use "like" or "as". (C) No opposite words are joined. (D) No sound is imitated.
Key point: "Like" or "as" signals a simile.

Question: According to the second stanza, why do the stars seem so bright?
options: A) The camels' bells have stopped ringing
B) The grandfather has lit a lantern nearby
C) There is no light from a city, lamp or window
D) The sand reflects the heat of the day
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) There is no light from a city, lamp or window
Why: "No city glare, no lamp, no window — / only the dark, so deep and wide / that every star burns like a lantern".
Why not the others: (A) and (D) belong to the first stanza and do not explain the brightness. (B) No lantern is lit.
Key point: Cause and effect can be linked by "so ... that".

Question: In "The Milky Way, a road of silver," the poet:
options: A) Describes a road that leads across the desert
B) Calls the band of stars a silver road
C) Names a road lit by silver lamps
D) Compares the Milky Way to a river of milk
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Calls the band of stars a silver road
Why: The Milky Way is called "a road of silver" running across the sky — a metaphor for the pale band of stars.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) take the line literally. (D) The poem says road, not river.
Key point: Read exactly what the figure compares.

Question: In the last stanza, the speaker feels "not less but larger" under the endless sky. This suggests that:
options: A) The speaker is proud of knowing the names of the stars
B) The speaker is frightened by the size of the sky
C) The speaker has grown taller since the last visit
D) The vast sky makes the speaker feel connected, not insignificant
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The vast sky makes the speaker feel connected, not insignificant
Why: One expects to feel small under an endless sky, but the speaker feels part of it — "as if the stars were watching, and so was I". The surprise is the point of the stanza.
Why not the others: (A) is not suggested. (B) The mood is wonder, not fear. (C) takes "larger" literally.
Key point: A line that contradicts what we expect usually carries the poem's meaning.
